Assess the case-drop stability of significant transitions

Source: R/stability_lsa.R
stability_lsa.Rd

stability_lsa() assesses the case-drop stability of the significant transitions of a fit from lsa(): whether a transition's significance survives when part of the data is left out, since a transition found significant in the full data may owe its significance to a few sequences. It follows the case-dropping approach that Epskamp, Borsboom and Fried (2018) describe for the stability of psychological networks: subsets of the cases are drawn without replacement, the model is refitted on each, and the share of subsets in which a transition is significant measures how much its significance depends on the particular cases sampled.

R subsets are drawn, each keeping a share proportion of the sequences (or, for a single sequence, a run of consecutive events of that share of its length); the model is refitted with the same engine and settings, and whether each transition is significant at the fit's alpha is recorded. A transition's stability is the share of subsets in which it was significant; it is flagged stable when that share reaches min_stable. Replicates in which a subset contained no transitions are reported as failed and count as not significant.

Stability concerns the significance decision, in either direction, not the size of the effect. For intervals on the statistics use bootstrap_lsa(); for a p-value against no sequential structure use permute_lsa(); for the agreement of the whole network between halves of the data use reliability_lsa().

Usage

stability_lsa(
  fit,
  R = 500L,
  proportion = 0.8,
  min_stable = 0.95,
  parallel = FALSE,
  n_cores = NULL,
  verbose = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

fit

An lsa fit from lsa(), built from sequences (not from a transition matrix).

R

Number of subsets. Default 500.

proportion

Share of the sequences kept in each subset, between 0 and 1. Default 0.8.

min_stable

Share of subsets in which a transition must be significant to be flagged stable, greater than 0 and at most 1. Default 0.95.

parallel

Run the subsets on several cores. Default FALSE.

n_cores

Number of cores when parallel = TRUE. Default NULL, all cores but one.

verbose

Report progress every 100 subsets. Default FALSE.

...

Not used.

Value

An object of class c("lsa_stability", "list"). Read it with transitions(), which returns a data frame with one row per transition (from -> to pair) and the columns from, to, observed_sig (significant in the full fit), stability (share of subsets in which it was significant) and stable (stability >= min_stable). transitions(x, significant = TRUE) keeps the stable transitions; sort = "strength" orders by stability. print() shows the settings, the number of failed replicates and the number of stable transitions (see lsa-inference-methods). The object also stores the per-subset significance decisions, the settings and the original fit.

Conditions

Errors carry the class lagdynamics_error and one of:

  • lagdynamics_needs_events: the fit was built from a transition matrix, so there are no sequences to drop.

References

Epskamp, S., Borsboom, D., & Fried, E. I. (2018). Estimating psychological networks and their accuracy: A tutorial paper. Behavior Research Methods, 50(1), 195-212.

See also

transitions() to read the result; bootstrap_lsa(), permute_lsa() and reliability_lsa() for other checks of a fit.

Examples

fit <- lsa(engagement)
st <- stability_lsa(fit, R = 100)
st
#> <lsa_stability>
#>   engine:        classical
#>   replicates:    100
#>   proportion:    80%
#>   min stable:    95%
#>   failed:        0 of 100 replicates
#>   stable edges:  7 of 9 (>= 95% across replicates)
transitions(st, significant = TRUE)
#>         from         to observed_sig stability stable
#> 1     Active     Active         TRUE         1   TRUE
#> 2    Average     Active         TRUE         1   TRUE
#> 3 Disengaged     Active         TRUE         1   TRUE
#> 4     Active    Average         TRUE         1   TRUE
#> 5    Average    Average         TRUE         1   TRUE
#> 6     Active Disengaged         TRUE         1   TRUE
#> 7 Disengaged Disengaged         TRUE         1   TRUE
# \donttest{
# A full analysis uses more subsets
stability_lsa(fit, R = 500, proportion = 0.5) |>
  transitions(sort = "strength")
#>         from         to observed_sig stability stable
#> 1     Active     Active         TRUE     1.000   TRUE
#> 2    Average     Active         TRUE     1.000   TRUE
#> 3 Disengaged     Active         TRUE     1.000   TRUE
#> 4     Active    Average         TRUE     1.000   TRUE
#> 5    Average    Average         TRUE     1.000   TRUE
#> 6     Active Disengaged         TRUE     1.000   TRUE
#> 7 Disengaged Disengaged         TRUE     1.000   TRUE
#> 8 Disengaged    Average        FALSE     0.248  FALSE
#> 9    Average Disengaged        FALSE     0.058  FALSE
# }
